name: X-ray hair removal

card.summary: A discontinued form of radiation epilation that permanently removed hair, used in the early twentieth century for scalp ringworm and for removing unwanted hair.
card.aka: X-ray epilation; roentgen-ray epilation; radiation epilation
card.note: Associated with later tumours and radiodermatitis; no longer practiced for cosmetic purposes and illegal for hair removal in the US.

quick.overview:
X-ray hair removal used doses of X-rays aimed at hair follicles to stop them producing hair, usually permanently. In appearance terms it offered smooth, hairless skin without repeated plucking or shaving, and in medicine it was used to clear the scalp of hair in children with tinea capitis (ringworm) so the infection could be treated.

Follow-up studies of irradiated children later reported excess tumours of the head and neck, and the method was abandoned. A reference text on hair removal describes it as effective and usually permanent, but also as causing severe health problems, occasional disfigurement and death, and it is illegal for hair removal in the United States.
quick.how: Historically it was carried out by physicians or technicians using X-ray equipment. For ringworm, a protocol known as the Kienbock-Adamson technique delivered a measured dose to the scalp, and the hair fell out about two weeks afterwards. Modern hair removal relies on lasers, intense pulsed light, electrolysis and waxing instead.
quick.risks: Long-term studies of people treated in childhood found more tumours of the skin, brain, thyroid and salivary glands, along with basal cell carcinoma and, in a case report, angiosarcoma, in irradiated areas. Radiodermatitis (chronic radiation skin damage) was also reported. The practice is discontinued.

lead: X-ray hair removal, also called X-ray or roentgen-ray epilation, is a discontinued method that exposed hair follicles to ionizing radiation so they stopped growing hair. It was described in a standard hair-removal textbook as an efficient and usually permanent method, which is how it was positioned for people who wanted lasting smoothness without regrowth [1].

The method was used medically as well. Through the mid-twentieth century, X-ray epilation of the scalp was a standard treatment for tinea capitis in children: a 1956 clinical article called it the most important single weapon against Microsporum audouini scalp infection because it shed the hair quickly and limited spread between children [2]. A related use was for severe scarring scalp disease such as dissecting cellulitis [3].

Later follow-up of thousands of treated children found increased rates of head and neck tumours, and the technique was abandoned [4][5]. Today it is listed among banned hair removal methods and is illegal in the United States [1].

chain: Follicles stop producing hair, often permanently
angle.text: The treatment worked by damaging follicles so hair did not return, giving lasting hairlessness. Because of the later tumour findings it is no longer used; current hair-reduction options such as lasers and electrolysis fill this role.

paras: The technique directed a measured exposure of X-rays at the scalp or skin so that hair follicles were destroyed or made dormant. Hair fell out some time after treatment, and in many cases did not grow back, which is why it was regarded as semi-permanent or permanent [1][2].

In the 1940s and 1950s, children with scalp ringworm were commonly treated with X-ray epilation. The 1956 article recommended it for children with the disease, stating that it could cure the infection quickly and halt spread, provided that competent technique and precautions were used; it named the Kienbock-Adamson technique [2].
Large follow-up cohorts were later assembled, including 2,215 people irradiated between 1940 and 1959 and 1,395 matched people treated without X-rays [4].

X-ray epilation was also reported as a treatment for dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, a scarring condition. A 1956 dermatology report described successful treatment [7], and a systematic review in 2021 noted that X-ray epilation and surgical excision showed the best remission rates for refractory cases but can carry serious morbidity [3]. A 1999 report suggested that laser-assisted hair removal might offer an alternative with less morbidity [8].

The 1976 follow-up of irradiated children found excess tumours of the head and neck, including skin, brain, thyroid and parotid gland [4]. A 1982 review of low-dose radiation risks noted that thyroid cancer and salivary gland tumours were among the diseases most consistently reported at low organ doses, and associated the first two with scalp X-ray epilation for tinea capitis [9].

Skin cancers also appeared in irradiated areas. A 1962 paper described basal cell carcinoma following scalp epilation [10], a 2012 study examined head and neck basal cell carcinoma prevalence in people irradiated in childhood [11], and a case report described scalp angiosarcoma arising in an area of radiodermatitis after childhood X-ray epilation [5]. A Spanish-language series of 77 scalp basal cell carcinoma patients found that 10 of 29 who were asked reported childhood X-ray epilation [12]. A 1978 follow-up also examined psychiatric and psychometric outcomes [13].

Studies are historical and mostly observational. They include cohort follow-ups of children irradiated for tinea capitis, which found excess head and neck tumours [4], plus case reports and series of skin cancers in irradiated scalps [5][10][12]. A 1956 clinical report supported use of the method for ringworm [2]. No modern trials exist for cosmetic X-ray hair removal.

timeline.event: Period in which a large cohort of children was treated by X-ray epilation for tinea capitis and later followed up [4].
A California medicine article describes X-ray epilation as the most important weapon against scalp ringworm [2].
Follow-up reports excess head and neck tumours in irradiated cohort [4].
Review links scalp epilation to thyroid and salivary gland tumours [9].
